summary: This experimental document describes ways to anonymize IP flow data and export anonymized data with IPFIX. It categorizes common schemes, defines parameters for describing them, and gives guidance on export and storage. An information model supports describing which fields were anonymized and how.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how to change sensitive fields in network-flow records before sharing them. It also defines IPFIX metadata that tells a recipient which fields were changed and how.

questions: how can ip flow data be anonymized
subtitle: Methods for anonymizing flow records and describing those methods in IPFIX exports.

tldr.problem: Sharing flow records can expose information about the networks, hosts, and users that generated the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes ways to transform sensitive fields and defines IPFIX metadata for identifying which anonymization methods were applied.
tldr.outcome: The Experimental RFC provides options and implementation guidance, but it does not endorse one method for every dataset or purpose.

today: RFC 6235 is Experimental. It describes anonymization techniques and metadata support for IPFIX, without recommending one technique for all uses.

sections.title: Why Flow Records Need Protection
sections.content:
IP flow records can help network operations, security, and research, but wider sharing can expose information about the people and systems represented in the data. Anonymization changes or removes sensitive information while trying to preserve properties useful for analysis.

The RFC focuses on techniques applied to individual fields in a flow record. It does not decide which technique is suitable for a particular purpose; publishers must consider their data and the risk that identities could be recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow records can reveal who or what communicated, even when the records are shared for analysis. Anonymization changes selected fields, but the publisher must choose a method that fits the data and its risks.

sections.title: Different Ways to Change Data
sections.content:
The RFC classifies anonymization by whether the original value can be recovered and whether the count of distinct values is preserved. Generalization maps multiple original values into a smaller set, while substitution replaces values with other values.

Techniques include truncating or permuting IP and MAC addresses, preserving address prefixes while pseudonymizing, reducing timestamp precision, shifting times, and changing counters through binning or noise. Deleting a field protects that field but also removes its analytical value.
sections.plainLanguage: Some methods remove detail, while others replace values with new ones. A method can preserve useful patterns, but keeping more structure can also leave clues that help identify the original data.

sections.title: Describing Changes in IPFIX
sections.content:
IPFIX uses templates to describe which fields appear in flow records. This RFC defines an anonymization options template and metadata information elements that describe which information element was changed, which technique was used, and relevant parameters.

The metadata can travel with exported records or be stored with IPFIX files. A recipient can use it to interpret the anonymized values and understand which transformations were applied.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX can carry a description of the anonymization alongside the changed flow data. That description identifies the affected field and the method used.

sections.title: Export, Storage, and Remaining Risk
sections.content:
The RFC gives guidance on applying anonymization before export or storage, including how to handle headers, options data, and configuration information. An exporter should keep the transformation description consistent with the data it produces.

Anonymization is not a complete privacy solution. Relationships across flows and other available information can help an attacker infer identities, so the RFC warns that a method's suitability depends on its context and threat of deanonymization.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing fields does not guarantee that a dataset can no longer identify anyone. Patterns across records or outside information may still reveal the original users or systems.
